The problem is not merely that Christianity has many denominations, the problem is that Christianity contains multiple layers of interpretive choice at the same time. On one level, there are thousands of denominational expressions. Gordon Conwell's Center for the Study of Global Christianity has long estimated roughly 45,000 denominations worldwide. On another level, those groups sit inside broad confessional families such as Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, and even Protestant. Then inside and across those sit contextual and liberationist frameworks like liberation theology, black theology, feminist theology, and related approaches. And beyond that are methodological frameworks such as political theology, process theology, and other revisionist or constructive approaches. That means the average Christian interpreter is never just reading the Bible. They're always reading through a stack of selections: a church tradition, a doctrinal inheritance, a social location, a philosophical method, and a moral priority structure. And that's where the cherry picking problem becomes devastating. Because once Christianity admits this many live frameworks, the claim that one believer is simply taking scripture seriously becomes much harder to sustain. One person foregrounds church authority, another foregrounds the poor, another foregrounds personal salvation, another foreground sacramental continuity, even another foregrounds gender justice or apocalyptic expectation, another foregrounds metaphysical coherence. All of them can still claim to be biblical because the real dispute is usually not whether the Bible contains material they can use, but which materials get centered, which gets subordinated, and which get explained away. The sheer plurality of current Christian families and theological methods makes that unavoidable. So the big point is this: Christian theology is structurally selective, not selectively abusive only in bad cases, but selective by design. Why? Because the source material is too large, too internally diverse, too historically layered, and too morally uneven to function without a framework. The framework decides what counts as central. And once the framework does that, biblical truth often turns out to mean in practice the portions of the tradition that best support the interpreters preferred moral, political, ecclesial, or existential commitments. Now this actually provides us with a three-layer critique.
